content: Calcium sulfate is a widely used chemical in both laboratory and industrial settings. In its γ-anhydrite form, which is nearly devoid of water, it serves as a desiccant to absorb moisture. It is also employed as a coagulant in food products like tofu. In its natural, unrefined state, calcium sulfate appears as a translucent, crystalline white rock. When marketed under the trade name Drierite, it is often blue or pink due to the addition of cobalt chloride, which acts as a moisture indicator. The hemihydrate form of calcium sulfate (CaSO4·0.5H2O) is commonly known as plaster of Paris, while the dihydrate form (CaSO4·2H2O) naturally occurs as gypsum. The anhydrous form, known as β-anhydrite, also occurs naturally. Depending on the method of calcination (heating) of calcium sulfate dihydrate, two specific hemihydrate forms can be produced: alpha-hemihydrate and beta-hemihydrate. These forms differ primarily in crystal size. Alpha-hemihydrate crystals are more prismatic and, when mixed with water, form a stronger and harder structure compared to beta-hemihydrate crystals. Calcium sulfate is also found in certain commercial products, such as Wonder Bread, where it serves as an additive. Commercial Production and Recovery The primary sources of calcium sulfate are naturally occurring gypsum and anhydrite, which are found worldwide as evaporite deposits. These materials can be extracted through open-cast quarrying or deep mining. Global production of natural gypsum is approximately 100 million tonnes annually. In addition to natural sources, calcium sulfate is produced as a by-product in several industrial processes: Flue Gas Desulfurization: Exhaust gases from fossil fuel power plants and other industrial processes, such as cement manufacturing, are treated with finely ground limestone or lime to reduce sulfur oxide emissions. This process produces calcium sulfite, which oxidizes to form calcium sulfate. Phosphoric Acid Production: When phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid, calcium sulfate precipitates as a by-product. Hydrogen Fluoride Production: Calcium fluoride is treated with sulfuric acid, resulting in the precipitation of calcium sulfate. Zinc Refining: Zinc sulfate solutions are treated with lime to co-precipitate heavy metals, including barium, along with calcium sulfate. Recycling from Drywall: Calcium sulfate can be recovered from scrap drywall at construction sites. It is important to note that these industrial processes often concentrate radioactive elements in the calcium sulfate by-product. This is particularly true for calcium sulfate derived from phosphate rock, as phosphate deposits naturally contain actinides. The phosphate industry alone generates over 200 million tonnes of calcium sulfate waste annually. Dehydration Reactions When gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) is heated to temperatures between 100°C and 150°C (212°F to 302°F), it undergoes partial dehydration, losing approximately 75% of its water content. Industrial calcination may involve temperatures as high as 170°C (338°F), at which point γ-anhydrite begins to form. The partially dehydrated product is known as calcium sulfate hemihydrate or calcined gypsum, commonly referred to as plaster of Paris (CaSO4·nH2O, where n ranges from 0.5 to 0.8). Dehydration begins at around 80°C (176°F), although in dry air, some dehydration can occur at temperatures as low as 50°C (122°F). During this process, the heat energy (heat of hydration) is primarily used to drive off water as vapor, rather than increasing the mineral's temperature. Once the water is fully removed, the temperature of the material rises more rapidly. This endothermic reaction is exploited in drywall to provide fire resistance. In the event of a fire, the water loss from the gypsum helps keep the structure behind the drywall relatively cool, thereby delaying damage to wooden or steel framing and reducing the risk of structural collapse. Unlike most minerals, which form liquid or semi-liquid pastes when rehydrated, calcined gypsum exhibits a unique property. When mixed with water at ambient temperatures, it rapidly reverts to its dihydrate form while simultaneously setting into a rigid and strong crystal lattice. This exothermic reaction allows gypsum to be easily molded into various shapes, such as sheets for drywall, sticks for blackboard chalk, and molds for immobilizing broken bones or for metal casting. When combined with polymers, calcined gypsum can also be used as a bone repair cement. Small amounts of calcined gypsum can be added to soil to create strong structures directly from cast earth, offering an alternative to adobe, which loses its strength when wet. By altering the conditions of dehydration, the porosity of the hemihydrate can be adjusted, resulting in alpha and beta hemihydrates, which are chemically similar but differ in physical properties. When heated to 180°C (356°F), the nearly water-free form of calcium sulfate, known as γ-anhydrite (CaSO4·nH2O, where n = 0 to 0.05), is produced. This form reacts slowly with water to revert to the dihydrate state, a property utilized in some commercial desiccants. At temperatures above 250°C (482°F), the completely anhydrous form, β-anhydrite, is formed. Unlike γ-anhydrite, β-anhydrite does not react with water, even over geological timescales, unless it is finely ground. The hemihydrate and γ-anhydrite forms of calcium sulfate have nearly identical crystal structures, which include channels capable of accommodating variable amounts of water or other small molecules, such as methanol. This structural similarity allows for easy interconversion between these forms.
